transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marta Alvarez (Nebula Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng), Samir Rao (CTO)

Summary (auto):
High-level discovery focused on model selection for multi-lingual customer-facing features, context length requirements (8k+), and tool-calling for live data pulls. Customer weighing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) given security and latency constraints. Action items captured for pricing, benchmarks, and technical deep-dive.

Topics: model tradeoffs; context windows; multilingual support; tool-calling (search/db connectors); deployment options (Hosted/Dedicated/Private); security (SOC2, KMS, SSO); latency vs cost tradeoffs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jared Kim: Okay, hi everyone, Jared from Redwood, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro, I'm Jared, AE, with Priya our SE.
[00:08] Marta Alvarez: Hi Jared, hi Priya. Marta here. Thanks for slotting us. We're evaluating options for a multi-lingual assistant in our product.
[00:16] Priya Desai: Hey Marta, hi all. Quick question up front — is the goal primarily customer support automation, or are you doing full product-facing generation?
[00:24] Marta Alvarez: It's a mix. Customer support first, but we want pro-active summaries and long-form policy explanations. Must support English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese.
[00:33] Samir Rao: Also must integrate with our internal search and a couple of transactional APIs — so tool-calling is a hard requirement.
[00:40] Liam O'Connor: From infra side, we have strict data residency for EU and US, SOC2 in place, and we rotate keys with HashiCorp Vault.
[00:49] Jared Kim: Great, that's helpful — I want to understand tradeoffs we typically see. Two big axes for you: context length and deployment model. You mentioned long-form and pro-active summaries — what are the longest contexts you expect?
[01:00] Marta Alvarez: For some cases, up to 8k tokens, but for thread-level summarization it could approach 16k occasionally. Typical sessions are 3-5k tokens.
[01:10] Priya Desai: Okay — so we should talk models that support 8k as baseline and variants that can do 16k. We also need to cover cost for running those contexts at scale.
[01:20] Samir Rao: On scale — we expect a few hundred QPS at peak across regions, but most are single-turn. The KV cache for threads could help.
[01:29] Jared Kim: Right, continuous KV caching can reduce redo tokens for long histories. For model families: open models like LlamaX/Meta derivatives, Mistral-like weights, and some quantized variants are typical. In Hosted we expose curated variants; Dedicated gives you reservation and predictable throughput; Private is for when you need full control over keys and network.
[01:46] Marta Alvarez: When you say curated variants, what's the difference vs self-hosting? We looked at a self-host play but worried about ops costs.
[01:53] Priya Desai: Curated means we've validated throughput/latency for specific families and provide quantized flavors with known cost/latency profiles. Self-hosting gives maximum control but pushes operational burden to your team — model updates, kernel tuning, GC, etc.
[02:06] Liam O'Connor: On compliance, we need audit logs and KMS integration, ideally HSM-backed keys. Do you support customer-managed keys?
[02:14] Jared Kim: Yes, for Private we support KMS integrations and HSM options. Dedicated can be configured with customer-managed KMS depending on contract. Hosted has envelope encryption and is SOC2 compliant, but customers often ask for Private when they need a full on-prem style control plane.
[02:29] Marta Alvarez: Latency is important — target 200-400ms for short assists and up to 2s for long summaries is acceptable. Is that realistic?
[02:37] Priya Desai: For short 1-2 turn prompts on a 8k model, 200-400ms is tight but achievable with Dedicated and proper batching guarantees and tuned kernels. Hosted also can hit it for smaller models; larger context windows usually bump latency.
[02:49] Samir Rao: Curious about tool-calling — we need a way to call search, pull data, and then have the model synthesize. Does Redwood support function calling and verifier steps?
[02:58] Priya Desai: Yes, we support function/tool calling patterns and can pass structured outputs back to your services. There's also the option to run tool invocations outside the model, then feed results back in — Redwood has tooling examples for both.
[03:10] Marta Alvarez: Any gotchas for multi-lingual performance? Some models degrade in Japanese.
[03:15] Priya Desai: Correct — not all open models are equally trained for every language. We recommend benchmarking your prompt sets across candidate models; we can run evals against your test prompts. Some models handle Spanish/Portuguese well, Japanese can be model-specific.
[03:26] Jared Kim: Also note tokenization differences across languages affect token counts; Japanese tokenization can blow past token budgets if not careful.
[03:33] [00:35] Marta Alvarez: Good point, we'll provide sample prompts.
[03:36] [04:00] Jared Kim: On cost — rough rule: longer context and larger models increase cost linearly-ish by tokens and model compute. Quantized 4-bit variants cut costs but may impact quality on certain tasks, esp. nuance-sensitive tasks like legal wording.
[04:13] Liam O'Connor: Does Redwood do automated quantization suggestions?
[04:16] Priya Desai: We have Redwood Optimize which suggests quantization profiles and batching configs per workload. We can propose a profile based on your evals.
[04:25] Samir Rao: For the pilot we want to compare at least three models: 8k open model (fast), 16k open model (capable of long context), and a smaller low-latency model for short assists. Can Redwood spin up a test harness?
[04:36] Priya Desai: Absolutely — we usually run a 2-week POC with sample traffic patterns. We can provide a benchmark harness, and Priya (SE) will share the spreadsheet.
[04:46] Marta Alvarez: For deployment, if we go Dedicated, can we configure reserved GPU pools in two regions? We want failover.
[04:53] Jared Kim: You can — Dedicated supports multi-region pools and failover routing. We can set autoscaling and burst policies. For strict data residency with on-prem data egress controls, Private is the stronger option.
[05:05] [05:15] Liam O'Connor: Networking: we prefer VPC peering and private endpoints. Any constraints?
[05:20] Priya Desai: VPC peering and private endpoints are standard for Private. For Dedicated we often configure private networking and can arrange peering with strict IP allowlists.
[05:29] Marta Alvarez: About observability — we need per-route latency breakdown and token cost per request.
[05:34] Jared Kim: Redwood Console gives per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost, and traces. We can export logs to your SIEM.
[05:41] Samir Rao: Security question — do you support granular RBAC and SSO?
[05:45] Priya Desai: Yes, SSO via SAML/OIDC and RBAC for roles. Private deployments can integrate with your existing IdP.
[05:52] [06:00] Marta Alvarez: Any known limitations for tool-calling in private deployments? Like external HTTP calls from the model runtime?
[06:07] Priya Desai: In Private we give you the control plane; depending on your network policy you can allow outbound calls, or you can run tool gateways internally. We also support mediation layers so model never directly calls external internet — the platform routes calls through your gateways.
[06:22] Jared Kim: Can I ask about success criteria for this project? Timeline?
[06:26] Marta Alvarez: We want an internal pilot in Q4, BAU rollout in Q1. Success for pilot is: 1) match or exceed current assistant accuracy, 2) meet latency SLOs, 3) pass security checklist for SOC2/keys.
[06:38] Samir Rao: Budget is still being shaped, but we'd prefer usage-based with a pathway to reserved capacity if performance warrants.
[06:45] Jared Kim: That aligns with Hosted->Dedicated transition. Start Hosted for quick validation, then move to Dedicated when you need throughput & SLOs, or Private if you need stronger control.
[06:56] [07:00] Liam O'Connor: Any client-side libraries or SDKs we should know about?
[07:03] Priya Desai: We have SDKs in Python/Node and a lightweight HTTP contract. For complex tool-calling we provide examples and middleware.
[07:11] Marta Alvarez: Can we get a sample flow where the model calls a search tool, we validate results, then model synthesizes?
[07:17] Priya Desai: Yes, we'll include a sample in the follow-up package.
[07:22] Jared Kim: Let's talk specific models — Priya, can you lay out a short recommendation set for their use-case?
[07:27] Priya Desai: Sure. Candidate A: an efficient 8k open model — good latency, decent multilingual. Candidate B: 16k variant tuned for long-context — higher cost, better for full-thread summarization. Candidate C: compact low-latency model for short assists — lower cost. For Japanese-sensitive tasks, we recommend an eval against Candidate B and maybe a proprietary model if needed. We'll provide sample metrics: tokens/sec, p50/p95 latencies, and normalized quality scores.
[07:52] Marta Alvarez: Any constraints around model updates and version pinning in a Dedicated or Private setup?
[07:58] Priya Desai: You can pin model versions and control rollouts. Dedicated gives you canary and A/B rollout support, and Private gives you full control.
[08:07] Samir Rao: If we needed on-prem, how invasive is the Private package?
[08:12] Jared Kim: Private on-prem is more involved — control plane components, networking setup, and careful capacity planning. We usually run a readiness assessment.
[08:21] [08:30] Marta Alvarez: For the POC, what telemetry do you collect and can we opt out of certain metrics?
[08:37] Priya Desai: We collect token-level stats, latencies, error rates; audit logs can be routed to you. You can opt out of telemetry beyond what is necessary for health and billing.
[08:47] Liam O'Connor: About dataset privacy — we don't want user messages to be used for model training.
[08:53] Jared Kim: Hosted has options; by default we do not use customer data to train public models. Private gives you complete isolation. We'll capture this in contract language.
[09:02] [09:15] Samir Rao: Who else from Redwood will we be working with?
[09:18] Jared Kim: You'll have SE support (Priya), solutions engineering for the pilot, and an assigned CSM if we move forward to Dedicated.
[09:26] Marta Alvarez: Can you outline the pilot metrics you recommend?
[09:29] Priya Desai: Accuracy vs baseline, latency p50/p95, token cost per session, tool-call success rate, and error rates for external calls. We'll include an evaluation plan in the follow-up.
[09:41] [09:45] Jared Kim: Quick recap of next steps — I'll send pricing and a pilot proposal. Priya will share the benchmark spreadsheet and a sample tool-calling flow. You'll share prompt sets and infra docs. Then we'll schedule a technical deep-dive.
[09:58] Marta Alvarez: Sounds good. One follow-up: do you have references for customers who did multilingual and tool-calling POCs?
[10:05] Priya Desai: Yes, we can share redacted case studies and a short list of references.
[10:10] Samir Rao: Awesome. Thanks, that's helpful.
[10:13] Jared Kim: Great — we'll send the materials and nail down timelines. Thanks everyone.
[10:18] Marta Alvarez: Thanks.
[10:19] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional timestamp markers are approximate; some speaker labels may be simplified. There are small transcription artifacts (e.g., model names heuristically transcribed as 'LlamaX').
